pbqs.title: Warehouse wireless rollout
scenario: A distribution center is adding three access points so handheld barcode scanners can reach the inventory system. The router (10.20.30.1) and switch SW1 (10.20.30.2) are already configured.
requirements: The SSID must be WH-Scanners, it must appear in the scanners' network list, and the key is Pallet#Scan24
The scanners support only 802.11g, and WPA2 with a pre-shared key (not WPA3); use the strongest security they support
The three access points must not interfere with each other
The access point subnet is sized for at most 14 devices
Match the AP uplinks to the switch ports to avoid a duplex mismatch
pbqs.instructions: Select each access point and the switch to review and change their settings. Changes save automatically.
explanation: In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap, so each AP takes a different one of them. 802.11g is the only 2.4 GHz option the scanners can join (802.11a and 802.11ac are 5 GHz; 802.11b is slower).
At most 14 devices means a /28 (255.255.255.240, 16 addresses, 14 usable). The APs need unused hosts from 10.20.30.3 to 10.20.30.14, because .1 is the router and .2 is SW1; the gateway is the router.

WPA2-Personal (AES) is the strongest option the scanners support; WEP and TKIP are deprecated. The switch ports are hard-coded to 100 Mb/s full duplex, so they do not negotiate. An AP left on auto would detect 100 Mb/s but fall back to half duplex: a duplex mismatch. Set the AP to 100/Full to match.

pbqs.title: Clinic staff Wi-Fi with 802.1X
scenario: A medical clinic is replacing its wireless network. Staff must sign in with their own directory accounts, and the RADIUS server NPS1 is already running. The access point management VLAN uses the subnet 172.16.60.0/27 with its gateway at 172.16.60.1.
requirements: SSID Clinic-Staff, visible to staff devices
Users authenticate individually through NPS1; some staff devices do not support WPA3
All staff devices support Wi-Fi 6; use the 5 GHz band only
Use only non-overlapping UNII-1 channels (36–48) at a width that lets all three APs use different channels
Each AP needs a management address in the AP subnet
pbqs.instructions: Select each access point (and NPS1 for its details) to configure the network. Changes save automatically.
explanation: Individual sign-in through RADIUS is 802.1X, which is WPA2-Enterprise (or WPA3-Enterprise, not offered here). WPA3-Personal and WPA2-Personal use one shared key. RADIUS authentication uses UDP 1812 (1813 is accounting).

802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) on 5 GHz is the fastest option every staff device supports. UNII-1 has four non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (36, 40, 44, 48); at 40 or 80 MHz the three APs would have to share spectrum.
A /27 is 255.255.255.224, with hosts 172.16.60.1–30; .1 is the gateway, so each AP takes a different unused host.

pbqs.title: Campus network build-out
scenario: A college is reorganizing three network zones behind its firewall. Place the right servers and devices in each zone and choose each zone's subnet: the smallest one that contains the zone's gateway address and has enough usable addresses.
requirements: Screened subnet: publish the college website over HTTPS and accept inbound email. Four addresses are needed in total, including the gateway 203.0.113.1

Building B: add three workstations for new staff and a wireless access point for laptops, and replace the Telnet server with a secure remote-administration server. Plan for 50 hosts; gateway 10.40.8.1
Data center: provide name resolution, central log collection and time synchronization. Plan for 13 hosts; gateway 172.20.5.1
pbqs.instructions: Select an object in the palette, then select an empty slot to place it; select a placed object to remove it. Objects can be used more than once and not every slot needs to be filled. Then choose each zone's subnet.
explanation: Public services belong in the screened subnet: a web server for HTTPS (443) and a mail server for inbound SMTP (25). Telnet sends credentials in clear text; SSH (22) replaces it. DNS (53), syslog (514) and NTP (123) are internal infrastructure, so they go in the data center.

Subnet sizing: usable hosts = 2^(32−prefix) − 2. Four hosts need a /29 (6 usable), 50 hosts a /26 (62), and 13 hosts a /28 (14). The subnet must also contain the gateway: 203.0.113.8/29 and 10.40.8.64/26 do not, and /30, /27 and /29 are too small for their zones.

pbqs.title: New branch office design
scenario: A new branch office needs three segments plus a small server closet. Place the servers and devices the requirements call for and choose each segment's subnet: the smallest that contains its gateway and fits the planned hosts.
requirements: Guest Wi-Fi: two access points for visitors; up to 100 clients; gateway 192.168.50.1
Security: three IP cameras and a device that records their video; 20 hosts planned; gateway 10.9.0.33
Staff LAN: two desk phones and a shared printer; 200 hosts planned; gateway 10.9.1.1
Server closet (no subnet to choose): automatic addressing for every segment, and 802.1X authentication for the staff LAN's switch ports
pbqs.instructions: Select an object, then select an empty slot to place it; select a placed object to remove it. Objects can be used more than once and not every slot needs to be filled. Then choose the subnets.
explanation: A network video recorder (NVR) stores the IP cameras' video. DHCP hands out addresses to every segment (with relay on the router), and RADIUS is the authentication server behind 802.1X.

Usable hosts = 2^(32−prefix) − 2: 100 clients need a /25 (126), 20 hosts a /27 (30) and 200 hosts a /24 (254). Gateway 10.9.0.33 sits in 10.9.0.32/27 (.32–.63), not 10.9.0.0/27 (.0–.31); a /28 holds only 14 hosts. 192.168.50.128/25 does not contain .1, and 10.9.0.0/23 contains 10.9.1.1 but is larger than needed.

pbqs.title: Replaced access switch
scenario: Switch SW3 on the engineering floor failed and was replaced with a new switch that still has its factory settings. SW1, the distribution switch, was changed during the outage and may also need attention.
requirements: Each device must reach only its correct network (see the VLAN list)
Disable every switch port that has nothing connected
The two links between SW1 and SW3 must form a single fault-tolerant connection
The links between SW1 and SW3 must carry only the VLANs that devices on SW3 use
Only make the changes needed to meet these requirements
pbqs.instructions: Select SW1 or SW3 to open its port table. Changes save automatically; the table starts with the configuration the switch has now. Cells that do not apply to a port (for example, the access VLAN of a trunk, or anything but the status of a disabled port) are not graded.
explanation: Each end device needs an access port in its own VLAN: the two workstations in 10, the printer in 20 and the camera in 30. A new switch puts every port in VLAN 1, which none of these devices use.

Two links between switches become one fault-tolerant connection with link aggregation (LACP, 802.3ad), so LACP must be enabled on both ports at both ends; SW1 Gi1/0/2 had it disabled. A link that carries several VLANs must be an 802.1Q trunk, and pruning it to 10, 20 and 30 keeps VLAN 40 (and the unused VLAN 1) off the floor. SW1 Gi1/0/2 was missing VLAN 30.
Unused ports are disabled so nobody can plug in an unauthorized device (port security, objective 5.5). The router port on SW1 was already correct and should be left alone.

pbqs.title: Front office phones and access points
scenario: A front office is moving to IP phones and two new access points on switch FO-SW. Each desk PC plugs into the back of its phone, so phone and PC share one switch port. Part of the port configuration was entered by a contractor and contains errors.
requirements: Phones must use the voice VLAN and the PCs behind them the data VLAN
Configure a voice VLAN only on ports that have a phone
Each access point is managed on the management VLAN, sent untagged, and serves the staff SSID (data VLAN) and the guest SSID Visitor (guest VLAN) as tagged traffic
Carry only the VLANs each access point needs
Disable every switch port that has nothing connected
pbqs.instructions: Select FO-SW to open its port table. Changes save automatically; the table starts with the configuration the switch has now. Cells that do not apply to a port (for example, the native VLAN of an access port, or anything but the status of a disabled port) are not graded.
explanation: A phone with a PC behind it uses an access port with two VLANs: the access (data) VLAN 10 for the PC's untagged frames and the voice VLAN 50, which the phone tags (learned through CDP/LLDP). FO-2 had the two swapped. The printer has no phone, so its port should not carry a voice VLAN.

An access point that serves several SSIDs needs an 802.1Q trunk. Its management traffic is untagged, so the native VLAN is 99, and the allowed list is 10, 60 and 99 (not 50: no phones on Wi-Fi, and not 1). AP-Lobby was an access port in the guest VLAN, which would put the AP and both SSIDs on guest; AP-Office had native VLAN 1 and was missing VLAN 60.
Unused ports are disabled (port security). The router uplink was already correct.

pbqs.title: SOHO connectivity troubleshooting
scenario: A small office reports that several PCs cannot reach the network while others work normally. All office devices belong on VLAN 10 (192.168.1.0/24). Auto-MDIX is turned off on both switches.
requirements: Review the cable test results first
Check each switch's port table and each device's IP configuration
For the server and every PC, choose the problem (or No problem) and the solution
pbqs.instructions: Select the cable tester, the switches, the server and the PCs to open them. Choose a problem and a solution for the server and every PC.
explanation: Wiremaps: PC1 shows pins 3 and 6 shorted together, PC5 is wired 1→8, 2→7 … (a connector on backward) and PC3 is a crossover cable. With Auto-MDIX off, a PC needs a straight-through cable to a switch, so PC3 has no link; the switch-to-switch uplink needs exactly the crossover it has. All three are fixed by replacing the cable.

PC6's run is 112 m, longer than the 100 m limit for twisted pair, which causes the CRC errors and the fallback to 100 Mb/s half duplex: replace it with a shorter run (or add a switch). PC4's cable and IP settings are fine, but its switch port is in VLAN 20 (cameras) instead of VLAN 10, so change the VLAN assignment.
Server 1 and PC2 have good straight-through cables under 100 m, link at 1000 Mb/s full duplex and correct settings: no problem.

pbqs.title: Office help-desk tickets
scenario: Several users in a small office opened tickets: some have no network at all, others can reach local devices but not the internet, and the printer cannot be reached. Every device is on VLAN 30 (10.50.4.0/24); the router is 10.50.4.1.
requirements: Review the cable test results, the switch port table and each device's IP configuration
For the NAS, the printer and every PC, choose the problem (or No problem) and the solution
pbqs.instructions: Select the cable tester, the switch, the NAS, the printer and the PCs to open them.
explanation: PC1's wiremap shows pin 2 open, so there is no link: replace the cable. PC2's cable tests good, but its switch port is administratively down (shut down): enable the port.

The printer's mask is 255.255.255.252 (/30), so its subnet is 10.50.4.40/30 (hosts 10.50.4.41–10.50.4.42) and the gateway 10.50.4.1 is outside it: change the mask to 255.255.255.0. PC4 points at 10.50.4.254, which is not the router, so it reaches local devices but not the internet: change the gateway address.
The NAS, PC3 and PC5 have no problem. PC5's 98 m run is within the 100 m limit and links at 1000 Mb/s, and the printer's 100 Mb/s link speed is normal for a printer.

pbqs.title: Secure remote administration ACL
scenario: You are writing the ACL that the core router applies to all traffic routed between the five segments below. Both the Linux servers and the web servers run Linux; the Windows servers run Windows Server. The router tracks connections, so return traffic for a permitted session is allowed automatically.
requirements: Administrators on the management network must reach every server segment using the most common secure remote-administration protocol for that segment's operating system
Users must reach the web servers over encrypted web traffic only
Users must not be able to open remote-administration sessions to any server segment
Block everything that has not been specifically permitted, with an explicit final rule
Do not permit anything broader than the requirements need (no "Any" where a segment will do)
pbqs.instructions: Select the router to open the ACL. Choose the source, destination, service and action for every rule.

blocks.title: Access control list (evaluated top to bottom, first match wins)

explanation: The most common secure remote-administration protocols are SSH (TCP 22) for Linux and RDP (TCP 3389) for Windows. Telnet and VNC are not encrypted by default. The web servers run Linux, so they are managed with SSH too.
Users get HTTPS (TCP 443) to the web servers only; plain HTTP is not encrypted. Because nothing else is permitted for users, the final deny already stops their SSH and RDP sessions to the servers.

Every permit names one source segment, one destination segment and one service, so none overlaps another and their order does not matter. The explicit deny any/any/any must be last: an ACL is read top to bottom and the first match wins, so a deny-all above a permit would block it.

pbqs.title: Branch services ACL
scenario: A branch router routes between four segments and filters that traffic with one ACL. The DNS and NTP servers and the intranet web server are all in the server segment; the network monitoring system is in the monitoring segment. The router tracks connections, so return traffic for a permitted session is allowed automatically.
requirements: Users must be able to resolve names with ordinary client DNS queries, and reach the intranet site over encrypted web traffic
The IP cameras must synchronize their clocks with the NTP server
The monitoring system must poll the cameras for status and counters
The cameras must send their log messages to the monitoring system
Block everything else with an explicit final rule, and permit nothing broader than needed
pbqs.instructions: Select the router to open the ACL. Choose the source, destination, service and action for every rule.

blocks.title: Access control list (evaluated top to bottom, first match wins)

explanation: Ordinary DNS client queries use UDP 53 (TCP 53 is for zone transfers and oversized responses). NTP uses UDP 123. Encrypted web traffic is HTTPS on TCP 443.

Polling devices for status and counters is SNMP: the monitoring system sends requests to UDP 161 on the cameras. Traps (UDP 162) flow the other way and are not polling. Log messages are syslog, UDP 514, from the cameras to the monitoring system.
The permits do not overlap, so their order does not matter; the explicit deny-all must be the last rule because the ACL stops at the first match.

requirements: Review the routing table on each router
For each router, state whether it has a problem
Where there is a problem, add one static route, for the destination subnet, that fixes it

The fix on Router C is a static route to 10.0.5.0 with mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) via Router A's address on their shared link, 172.16.27.1. Router A already reaches site B through its default route, and Router B already reaches site A through its default route, so neither needs a change.

scenario: A company connects two branch offices to headquarters over point-to-point links; HQ has the only internet connection. Branch 2 users (192.168.30.0/24) can reach the HQ servers (192.168.10.0/24), but not Branch 1 or internet sites such as 198.51.100.80. Branch 1 users can reach HQ and the internet. Routing is static.
requirements: Review the routing table on each router
For each router, state whether it has a problem
Where there is a problem, add the single static route that restores all of the missing access
pbqs.instructions: Select each router. Its first tab shows the routing table; the second is where you record a problem and the route to add. Leave the route empty on routers that need no change.

pbqs.title: Department addressing faults
scenario: Some devices in a small office cannot reach the network or other departments, while others work. Every device is configured statically, and each department has its own VLAN and subnet.
requirements: Review the VLAN plan, the switch port assignments and each device's IP configuration
For every device, choose the problem (or No problem) and the solution
pbqs.instructions: Select VLANs (the usage plan), the switch and each device to open them. Choose a problem and a solution for every device.
explanation: Server1's gateway is 10.10.5.254, but the router's address in the server VLAN is 10.10.5.1: change the gateway. PC2 uses a /25 mask, so its subnet is 10.10.4.128/25 and the gateway 10.10.4.1 is outside it: change the mask to /24.

PC3 is in HR and has an HR address, but its switch port is in VLAN 30 (Marketing): change the VLAN assignment. PC5 is in HR and on VLAN 20, but its address 10.10.3.15 is from the Marketing subnet: change the IP address.
PC4 points at 10.10.5.35 for DNS instead of Server1 (10.10.5.53), so it reaches hosts by address but cannot resolve names: change the DNS address. PC1 and the printer match the plan.

pbqs.title: Second-floor connectivity
scenario: The DHCP server for the staff VLAN was offline this morning and has now been restored, but some devices on the second floor still cannot connect. Staff laptops and PC1 use DHCP; every other device is configured statically. On this floor the router is always the .254 address of each subnet.
requirements: Review the VLAN plan, the switch port assignments and each device's IP configuration
For every device, choose the problem (or No problem) and the solution
pbqs.instructions: Select VLANs (the usage plan), the switch and each device to open them. Choose a problem and a solution for every device.
explanation: Laptop1 has a 169.254.x.x (APIPA) address: it self-assigned one when DHCP got no answer and keeps it until its next retry. Release and renew its address to get a lease now that the server is back. PC1 got a correct lease.

PC2 points at 172.20.10.1, but the router is 172.20.10.254: change the gateway. PC3's address 172.20.10.255 is the broadcast address of 172.20.10.0/24 and cannot be assigned to a host: change the IP address.

Printer1 has a /16 mask, so it treats every 172.20.x.x address (including the staff and server subnets) as local and never sends that traffic to its gateway: change the mask to /24. Printer2's settings are right, but its switch port is in the staff VLAN 110 instead of 130: change the VLAN assignment. FS1 matches the plan.

pbqs.title: Monitoring after a power outage
scenario: Power failed at 02:14 last night and was restored at 02:20. Since then users report that the application server is slow, and users in the east wing have weak or no Wi-Fi. The network monitoring dashboard is shown below.
requirements: Open each dashboard tab and review the widgets
Answer every question under the dashboard
pbqs.instructions: Use the tabs above the dashboard to switch views. The questions stay visible below it.

widgets.text: The app server NIC is hard-coded to 100 Mb/s full duplex. WAP1 covers the west wing and WAP2 the east wing.

fields.label: Which WAN uplink should be preferred for VoIP traffic?
Which device explains the east-wing Wi-Fi problem?
What is the most likely cause of the slow application server?
options: Duplex mismatch on the app server's switch port
A switching loop on Switch A
The app server is low on memory
fields.answer: Duplex mismatch on the app server's switch port

fields.label: Which internal host is generating the most traffic?

explanation: VoIP needs low loss, latency and jitter more than bandwidth. WAN1 has more capacity but 2.51 % loss, above the 1 % guideline; WAN2 has 0.01 % loss, 11 ms latency and 3.9 ms jitter, so it should carry voice.
WAP2 has been down since 02:14 and its switch port shows PoE power denied, which is why the east wing has weak or no Wi-Fi (clients there reach only the distant WAP1). Every other device is up.

After the outage the app server's switch port came back on auto-negotiation. Facing a NIC hard-coded to 100 Mb/s full duplex (which does not negotiate), it detected 100 Mb/s but fell back to half duplex: a duplex mismatch. Late collisions are its signature, and the port is saturated at 97 %.
203.0.113.45 sends the most bytes, but it is an external host (the backup provider), not one of ours. The busiest internal host is 10.1.90.53.

pbqs.title: School network health check
scenario: On Monday morning teachers report that everything is slow, a computer lab PC keeps losing its connection, and Wi-Fi in the science wing is sluggish even close to the access point. Use the monitoring dashboard for the main building switch and wireless network.
requirements: Open each dashboard tab and review the widgets
Answer every question under the dashboard
pbqs.instructions: Use the tabs above the dashboard to switch views. The questions stay visible below it.

fields.label: Which port is the bottleneck making everything slow?
Which port has a physical-layer (cabling) problem?
What do the syslog messages indicate?
What is the most likely cause of the slow science-wing Wi-Fi?
options: Too many clients for one AP
The AP is on the wrong band

explanation: The uplink to the core, Gi1/0/48, is at 98 % utilization, so everything that leaves the building queues behind it. Gi1/0/12 (the lab PC) has thousands of CRC errors at full duplex with no late collisions: corrupted frames from a bad cable or connector, not a duplex mismatch.

The same MAC addresses flapping between Gi1/0/5 and Gi1/0/6 (two wall jacks in room 104, both busy at about 60 %) means frames loop between them: someone has connected the two jacks, for example through a small switch. That is a switching loop. The config message is a normal admin login.

AP3 shares channel 6 with AP2 on the other side of the wall, and its channel utilization is 87 %. SNR (34 dB) and the client count (24 of 60) are fine, so the cause is co-channel interference: move AP3 to a free non-overlapping channel.

explanation: show cdp neighbors detail gives the access point's and phones' interfaces and IP addresses. A Cisco phone's CDP device ID is SEP followed by its MAC, so SEP0200AA000101 is Phone-101 (Gi1/0/3, 10.40.50.31) and SEP0200AA000102 is Phone-102 (Gi1/0/7, 10.40.50.32). The phones' DHCP bindings are in VLAN 50, the voice VLAN.

AP-East is on Gi1/0/24 (10.40.99.21); show interfaces trunk shows that port's native VLAN is 99. The printer does not run CDP, but the DHCP snooping table lists its MAC (shown as 02:00:00:BB:00:42) with 10.40.10.88 in VLAN 10 on Gi1/0/15. The 10.40.10.57 binding on Gi1/0/3 is the PC behind Phone-101, not the phone.
